paragraphs: §1 — Gen 1:26: naʿaseh adam and kidmutenu (the plural and the likeness)

The first of that is His statement in the Torah [Gen 1:26]: וַיֹּאמֶר אֱלֹהִים נַעֲשֶׂה אָדָם. They cling, from this, to two words: the first is His saying נַעֲשֶׂה ("let us make") — which is in the diction of plurality (bi-lisān taktīr), and this — on their view — indicates more than one; and that "more than one" is the aqānīm [hypostases]. The second is His saying [same place]: כִּדְמוּתֵנוּ ("in our likeness") — and this — on their view — indicates that the Creator (sublime be His praise) resembles human beings, by which He intended one of the hypostases (namely Jesus), since [Jesus] became united with the body of a human.

: Gen 1:26 is the foundational Christian Hebrew-Bible prooftext for the Trinity, and Q's presentation of the argument is standard for 9th-10th-century Christian apologetic. The cotextual move from naʿaseh ("let us") to the aqānīm requires both (i) reading the plural-of-majesty form naʿaseh as a true ontological plural, and (ii) reading kidmutenu ("in our likeness") as foreshadowing the Incarnation. Q records both moves cleanly here without comment; the refutations (the plurale maiestatis reading; kidmut as "image" not "physical likeness"; the aggadic reading of naʿaseh as God consulting the angels) are reserved for Bab 6. Christian-side Vorlage: the naʿaseh-plural argument is a standard fixture of the 9th-10th-c. Arabic-Christian apologetic tradition Q is engaging — Theodore Abū Qurra (d. ca. 830) and ʿAmmār al-Baṣrī (early 9th c.) both rehearse it in their Trinitarian mayāmir and masāʾil. Yaḥyā b. ʿAdī (d. 974) — Q's most direct contemporary Christian apologist target — gives the same argument in his Maqāla fī al-Tawḥīd (Perier ed., scattered through the Trinité section). The Bahshamī refutation Q will deploy in Bab 6 is preserved in SUK 5371-5505 in its anti-Christian section, though without engaging Gen 1:26 specifically — Bahshamī polemicists tended to attack the doctrine of ittihād and tathlīth in the abstract rather than verse-by-verse, leaving the exegetical work to Karaite and Rabbanite specialists.
§2 — Gen 49:10: the scepter shall not depart from Judah, until Shiloh comes

And of that, His saying [Gen 49:10]: לֹא יָסוּר שֵׁבֶט מִיהוּדָה, and His saying [same place]: עַד כִּי יָבֹא שִׁילֹה ("until Shiloh comes"). They said: He informs that the scepter of kingship (qaḍīb al-mulk) shall not depart from Judah until the one who is his comes — and that one is Jesus, who is the Messiah. What confirms this for them is His saying [same place]: וְלוֹ יִקְּהַת עַמִּים ("and to him shall be the obedience of the peoples") — meaning that all the nations shall submit to him and acknowledge him.

: Gen 49:10 was the central Christian messianic prooftext in 9th-10th-century Christian-Jewish disputation. The pivot is the cryptic word Shiloh (שִׁילֹה), which Christians read as a proper noun referring to the Messiah (either as place — Bethlehem-environs — or as ad hoc theonym), supported by the LXX rendering ἕως ἂν ἔλθῃ τὰ ἀποκείμενα αὐτῷ ("until comes the things laid up for him"). The Jewish (and Karaite) reading takes Shiloh as a place name (Joshua's Shiloh) or as שֶׁלוֹ ("that which is his"). Q here reports faithfully — the refutation, again, comes in Bab 6. The Karaite tradition's treatment of Gen 49:10 — running from Q through Yefet ben ʿEli's commentary on Genesis — is treated at length in M.A. Friedman, Peamim (2018) on the Christian use of Gen 49:10 (per anchor grid); see also Lasker, Jewish Philosophical Polemics (2nd ed.), Ch. 5.
§3 — Isa 7:14 (the almah and the virgin birth) + Isa 48:16, Isa 63:10, 2 Sam 23:2 (for the Holy Spirit)

And of that, the saying of Yeshaʿyāhū [Isa 7:14]: הִנֵּה הָעַלְמָה הָרָה וְיֹלֶדֶת בֵּן וְקָרָאת שְׁמוֹ עִמָּנוּאֵל ("Behold the ʿalmā is pregnant and bears a son and shall call his name Immanuel"). They claimed that the ʿalmā [maiden] is Maryam [Mary], and that she bore [a son] without a man having had intercourse with her — and this is the wondrous sign (al-āya al-ʿajība); for otherwise, who is this maiden who has borne a son such that that should be a wondrous sign?

And they cite, for what they have claimed of the Holy Spirit (rūḥ al-qudus), the saying of Yeshaʿyāhū (peace be upon him) [Isa 48:16]: וְעַתָּה אֲדֹנָי אֱלֹהִים שְׁלָחַנִי וְרוּחוֹ ("and now the Lord God has sent me, and His spirit"). They claimed that he intended: God and His spirit have sent me. And the like of that, for them, is His saying [Isa 63:10]: וְהֵמָּה מָרוּ וְעִצְּבוּ אֶת רוּחַ קָדְשׁוֹ ("and they rebelled and grieved His holy spirit"); and the saying of Dod [David], peace be upon him [2 Sam 23:2]: רוּחַ יְיָ דִּבֶּר בִּי ("the spirit of the Lord spoke through me").

: The Christian appropriation of Isa 7:14 as a Virgin-Birth prooftext goes back to Matthew 1:23, which quotes the LXX's παρθένος ("virgin") for ʿalmā — a translation Jewish (and Karaite) polemicists have always disputed on philological grounds, since ʿalmā means "young woman" or "marriageable girl," not specifically "virgin" (the technical word for which would be betūlā). Q's parenthetical "for otherwise, who is this maiden who has borne a son such that that should be a wondrous sign?" is the Christian rhetorical question: if not a virgin, why would this be a sign at all? Q records it; the refutation (a young woman of Yeshaʿyāhū's own time, on the standard Karaite reading) is reserved for Bab 6. The most likely Christian-side Vorlage in Q's immediate Arabic milieu is Theodore Abū Qurra's Mayāmir (Bacha ed., d. ca. 830 CE), where Maryam al-ʿadhrāʾ (Mary the Virgin) is repeatedly invoked as the hinge of the Christological argument (lines 344, 1065, 1208, 1332-1349, 1418, 1450-1456 of the Bacha ed. text). Abū Qurra's distinctive formulation — al-azalī wulida min Maryam al-ʿadhrāʾ ("the pre-eternal one was born from the Virgin Mary," ll. 1333, 1349) — is the kind of formulation that lies behind Q's fa-zaʿamū anna al-jāriya hiya Maryam wa-annahā waladat min ghayr an yuwāqiʿahā rajul. The Karaite-Rabbanite philological refutation surfaces fully in Yefet ben ʿEli's commentary on Isaiah ad loc.; Saadia's lost anti-Christian polemic also addressed this verse (cited by ʿAbd al-Jabbār, Mughnī* Vol. 5).

: The "Holy Spirit" prooftext trio (Isa 48:16, Isa 63:10, 2 Sam 23:2) is the standard Christian-apologetic set for the third hypostasis. All three are scripturally legible as poetic personification of God's rūaḥ. Q records the Christian reading without engaging the disambiguation; again, the refutation in Bab 6.
§4 — Ps 2:7, Ps 2:12, Ps 110:1 (the "Son" and the Father-Son relation)

They also cling to the saying of David in [Ps 2:7]: יְיָ אָמַר אֵלַי בְּנִי [אַתָּה] ("the Lord said to me: 'You are my Son'") — that He intended by this Jesus, who is the Son. And his saying [Ps 2:12]: נַשְּׁקוּ בַר ("kiss the son") — its meaning, on their view, is kiss the son, i.e., kiss the Messiah, who is the Son of God. And of that, his saying [Ps 110:1]: נְאֻם יְיָ לַאדֹנִי שֵׁב לִימִינִי ("an utterance of the Lord to my Lord: sit at my right hand") — the meaning of this, for them, is that God said to the Messiah (who is Jesus): sit at My right hand.

: Ps 2 and Ps 110 form, with Isa 7:14 and Isa 53, the bedrock of the Christian Hebrew-Bible Christology. Ps 110:1 in particular is the verse Jesus is reported to engage in Matt 22:41-46 par., and it dominates the Christian Christological reading from the Apostolic age forward (cited e.g. some 21 times in the New Testament). Q's report of the Christian gloss is precise and economical. The Karaite refutational tradition — Q's own in Bab 6, plus Yefet ben ʿEli's much fuller treatment in his Psalms commentary — runs as follows: Ps 2 is a coronation Psalm of the Davidic king (in the standard ANE adoption-formula); Ps 110:1 is David addressing his own future Davidic adonai, who is a mortal king, not God; bar in Ps 2:12 may not be Aramaic for "son" at all but Hebrew for "purity" (cf. the JPS marginal note). The verse-by-verse refutations are reserved for Bab 6.
§5 — Ps 56:11 (baʾElohim ahallel davar — for the pre-eternity of the Word)

They cite, for what we have recounted [in Bab 3] of the pre-eternity of the Word (qidam al-kalima), his saying [Ps 56:11]: בֵּאלֹהִים אֲהַלֵּל דָּבָר ("In God I praise the Word"). Its meaning, on their view: the pre-eternal Word (al-kalima al-qadīma) which is with God, and which is God. This is the head of what they rely on in argumentation, and what we have not mentioned of Scripture besides this is close to it.

: Reading dāvār (דָּבָר) in Ps 56:11 as the eternal Logos / kalima is a clear Christianized exegesis: dāvār in Biblical Hebrew is "word" or "matter / thing," and in the context of Ps 56:11 it is most naturally rendered "In God I praise that-which-He-has-spoken" (= His promise), parallel to "In the Lord I praise his word" of v. 11b. The Christian appropriation runs dāvār = logos = the second hypostasis. Q's gloss "the pre-eternal Word which is with God, and which is God" precisely captures the Christian commitment — and almost paraphrases the prologue to John 1:1 (καὶ ὁ λόγος ἦν πρὸς τὸν θεόν, καὶ θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος). The closing remark — "this is the head of what they rely on, and what we have not mentioned is close to it" — is Q's signal that he has presented the principal Christian Christological prooftext-set; further verses they adduce are variants on the same patterns and do not require separate cataloguing.
§6 — Deut 10:12 and Mic 6:8 (the "true commandment" is fear, kindness, humility — not law)

And what they cite for [the claim] that the commandments of the Torah are not pleasing, and that the true commandment (al-farḍ al-ḥaqq) which God wants from people and seeks is piety and humility (al-khashiya wa-l-tawāḍuʿ) — His saying [Deut 10:12]: וְעַתָּה יִשְׂרָאֵל מָה יְיָ אֱלֹהֶיךָ שֹׁאֵל מֵעִמָּךְ כִּי אִם לְיִרְאָה [אֶת יְיָ אֱלֹהֶיךָ], etc. ("and now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you but to fear [the Lord your God], etc."); and His saying [Micah 6:8]: הִגִּיד לְךָ אָדָם מָה טּוֹב וּמָה יְיָ דּוֹרֵשׁ מִמְּךָ כִּי אִם עֲשׂוֹת מִשְׁפָּט וְאַהֲבַת חֶסֶד וְהַצְנֵעַ לֶכֶת עִם אֱלֹהֶיךָ ("He has told you, O man, what is good, and what the Lord requires of you, but to do justice, to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God").

They said: It has become clear in these two places that what God wants and requires from people is piety (al-khashiya), the working of al-maʿrūf (kindness, the customary good), and humility (al-tawāḍuʿ) — and nothing else.

: The Christian use of Deut 10:12 and Mic 6:8 as anti-legal prooftexts is a fixture of the Pauline-patristic supersessionist tradition (compare Paul's appeal to Hab 2:4 in Rom 1:17 and Gal 3:11), but the specific Deut 10:12 + Mic 6:8 + Hos 6:6 triad surfaces especially in the 9th-10th-century Arabic-Christian apologetic where Q would have encountered it. The Jewish-Karaite refutation (again, deferred to Bab 6) runs: these verses describe the dispositional orientation that the legal commandments are designed to produce — not a substitute for the law. Q's note that this is the Christian case (not his own) is important — he is presenting, not endorsing. For the Arabic-Christian Vorlage see Theodore Abū Qurra's Mīmar fī Wujūd al-Khāliq wa-l-Dīn al-Qawīm and his Mīmar fī Sharāʾiʿ al-Naṣārā (both in the Bacha edition), where Mic 6:8 and the priority of dispositional virtues over ritual commandments is rehearsed in similar terms. For the Karaite refutational tradition that Q's Bab 6 will continue, the most fully-developed treatment is in Yefet ben ʿEli's commentary on Micah (early 11th c.) — Yefet works through the entire prophetic-vs-priestly construction systematically. For modern critical history of the Christian use of Jer 7:22 specifically, see Walter Brueggemann ad loc.; for the medieval Jewish response, see Y. Kaufmann's Religion of Israel (abridged ed.) ch. 3.
§7 — The Saul-kingship episode, the wilderness un-circumcision, and Jer 7:22 (sacrifices were not commanded)

They also rely on the affair of kings (amr al-mulūk) and the Scripture's statement [Deut 17:15]: שׂוֹם תָּשִׂים עָלֶיךָ מֶלֶךְ ("you shall surely set over yourself a king") and its remainder — together [with the fact] that, alongside this saying, He was averse (kāriha) to their request for him [a king]; and that is clear in the story of Shemūʾēl [Samuel, in 1 Sam 8], peace be upon him.

They also cite the failure of the Children of Israel concerning circumcision (al-khitāna) in the wilderness, and that they were not reproached for that, nor did wrath fall upon them — for in their view, had the commandment regarding it been a pleasing matter, they would have had to be censurable and reproached and not-pleasing in their failing-to-perform-it.

They also cling to the commandment of the sacrifices (al-qarābīn), and [argue] that this was not pleasing — for He says [Jer 7:22]: כִּי לֹא דִבַּרְתִּי אֶת אֲבוֹתֵיכֶם וְלֹא צִוִּיתִים בְּיוֹם הוֹצִיאִי אֹתָם מֵאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם ("for I did not speak to your fathers nor command them on the day I brought them out of the land of Egypt…") [text trails off; the verse continues "…concerning matters of burnt offering and sacrifice"].

: The "kings" prooftext is interesting: Deut 17:15 commands the appointment of a king, but 1 Sam 8 has God expressing reluctance ("they have not rejected you but Me") at Israel's request for one. The Christian argument — if a commanded thing can be displeasing-when-asked-for, then commands as such are not transparently divine-pleasing — turns on this apparent tension. The Karaite refutation distinguishes between the commandment (good in itself) and the manner of asking (which expressed faithlessness); Q's full treatment is in Bab 6.

: The Joshua 5:2-7 narrative — that the wilderness-generation Israelites were not circumcised, and that this was rectified at Gilgal after the Jordan crossing — is a thin reed for the Christian argument: the reason given (Joshua 5:5-6) is that the generation died in the wilderness and their children were the ones who needed circumcision post-crossing. The Christian argument repurposes this as evidence that circumcision was not strictly enforced and is therefore not really pleasing — a reading Q's refutation (Bab 6) will treat as historically tendentious.

: Jer 7:22 is the most-cited Hebrew Bible prooftext for the prophetic-against-the-priestly construction of Israelite religion that became standard in Christian (and later modern critical) historiography. Read super-literally, it appears to deny that sacrifices were divinely commanded at the exodus — though the immediate context (Jer 7:21-23) makes clear Jeremiah's point is the prioritization of obedience over ritual, not the rejection of ritual per se. The Karaite refutation (Bab 6) will likely follow the rabbinic-medieval line: the verse is a priority claim ("not [primarily] sacrifice, but obedience"), not a historical claim. Note that the bab ends mid-verse — the continuation "concerning matters of burnt offering and sacrifice" (ʿal divrei ʿōlā wa-zevaḥ) is on the OCR-pending p295, which falls in the Bab 6 range.

- The bab's expository character. Bab 5 is structurally unique within Maqala III: it does not refute anything. It is a catalogue — Q assembles the Christian biblical case in a single sustained presentation, with no rebuttals or rejoinders mixed in, before turning to the systematic refutation in Bab 6. The methodological commitment Q is performing is Bahshamī-rationalist: give the opponent's case a fair full hearing before you knock it down. The closest stylistic parallel in the Bahshamī corpus is ʿAbd al-Jabbār's Mughnī Vol. 5 (al-Firaq Ghayr al-Islāmiyya), where the Christian biblical and rational arguments are likewise catalogued before the systematic refutation. Q's framing is even more explicit, however — the bab heading literally is "On the recounting of what they cite from Scripture."

- The fourfold doctrinal structure of the catalogue. Q's selection of prooftexts maps cleanly onto four Christian-apologetic clusters: 1. Trinity (§1: Gen 1:26 — the naʿaseh plural) 2. Christological messianism (§§2-4: Gen 49:10 Shiloh; Isa 7:14 almah; Ps 2:7 bnī attā; Ps 2:12 nashqu bar; Ps 110:1 shev limini) 3. The Holy Spirit as hypostasis (§3 sub-cluster: Isa 48:16; Isa 63:10; 2 Sam 23:2) 4. The pre-eternity of the Word / Logos (§5: Ps 56:11)

Plus a fifth cluster on the non-bindingness of Torah law (§§6-7), comprising: - The "true commandment is piety/humility" cluster (Deut 10:12 + Mic 6:8) - The "commandments are sometimes not pleasing" cluster (Deut 17:15 + 1 Sam 8 / Joshua 5 circumcision lapse / Jer 7:22 sacrifices).

- The "head and the tail" hint (§5 close). Q says he has given "the head of what they rely on; what we have not mentioned is close to it" (hādhā raʾs mā yaʿtamidūna ʿalayhi…wa-mā lam nadhkurhu min al-kitāb qarīb min hādhā). This signals that he is presenting the principal Christian prooftext-set — the standardly-cited verses — but is not claiming exhaustiveness. The further Christian Christological verses (e.g., Isa 9:5 ʿEl gibbor, Isa 53 the suffering servant, Mal 3:1 the messenger of the covenant, Dan 7:13 one like a son of man) are not catalogued here. Bab 16, dedicated to refuting the prophethood of Jesus (Nemoy 1930 HUCA 7), addresses some of them.

- Q's Christian-apologetic Vorlage. The catalogue Q reports is virtually identical to the one that surfaces in Theodore Abū Qurra's Mīmar fī al-Tathlīth wa-l-Tawḥīd and in ʿAmmār al-Baṣrī's Kitāb al-Burhān and Kitāb al-Masāʾil wa-l-Ajwiba (early 9th c.), and continues into Yaḥyā b. ʿAdī's 10th-c. Maqāla fī al-Tawḥīd. The same verses (Gen 1:26 naʿaseh, Gen 49:10 Shiloh, Isa 7:14 almah, Ps 110:1 shev limini, Ps 2:7 bnī attā) appear in their Trinitarian and Christological prooftext-lists. This is strong indirect evidence that Q is engaging the Arabic-Christian apologetic tradition of his own day rather than (or in addition to) earlier Syriac or Greek sources.

- The "we will show…" promise (§4 close). Q's deferred-refutation promise — "We shall display the corruption of this dissimulation, and show the otherworldly reward and punishment from the Torah and the other books of the prophets" — frames Bab 6 as the delivery of what Bab 5 set up. This rhetorical architecture (catalogue → refutation) means Bab 5 and Bab 6 should be read as a single argumentative unit, the longest such unit in Maqala III.

- The Karaite stake. It bears mention that the Christian anti-legal prooftexts of §§6-7 are not narrowly anti-rabbinic but anti-Torah-as-such. For Q the Karaite — who has built his religious identity around the Torah as written against the Rabbanite Oral Torah — the Christian challenge bites differently than it does for a Rabbanite. The Karaite cannot retreat to "the Torah-of-the-heart" or rabbinic legal-spiritualization; he must show that the written commandments are the divinely pleasing forms of obedience. Q's refutational strategy in Bab 6 will likely emphasize the literal (ẓāhir) sense of the prophetic-spiritualization verses (Mic 6:8, Hos 6:6) as compatible with — not opposed to — strict legal observance.
